rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word describes arrogant rejection of truth and rebellion brought on by ingratitude for God’s favours, as exemplified by the destroyed people of 28:58.
rows.anchor: to show haughtiness before the truth and to turn away from it in arrogance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning against Quraysh’s attitude continues the earlier command to remember God abundantly.
rows.anchor: go against what they were asked to do earlier: remembering God in abundance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people described by the phrase are the Quraysh, who came to Badr with pomp and pretension.
rows.anchor: The words “like those who” refer to the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh’s confidence rested on its numbers and resources; believers must be humble as worshippers, since their warfare is worship and must retain its dignity.
rows.anchor: Their arrogance was due to their large number and copious means and resources. Believers are told not to adopt this attitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers should rely on God’s presence and help rather than their own growing numbers or resources, and stay alert for future trials.
rows.anchor: These resources are not the real thing; God’s company and help are the real thing which believers should rely upon.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning anticipates trials: a faction’s dispute at Uḥud endangered the army, while conceit over numbers brought a severe trial at Ḥunayn, as 9:25 recounts.
rows.anchor: on the occasion of the battle of Ḥunayn the believers faced a great trial because of showing conceit on their large number.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Badr, “boastfully” describes the pretentiousness of every Quraysh leader; its opposite is sincerity.
rows.anchor: The word “boastfully” refers to the pretentiousness with which each and every leader of the Quraysh in the battle of Badr was overcome with.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers should act only to please God and earn the Hereafter’s reward, not to win worldly praise.
rows.anchor: whatever they undertake must be solely to please God and to earn reward in the Hereafter and not to earn any worldly praise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about obstructing God’s way explains the Quraysh’s pomposity; the reminder that God encompasses their actions shows their achievements remain under His control.
rows.anchor: these foolish people do not know that however much human beings may expand the circle of their achievements they are always in the control of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh’s arrogance was fueled by their abundance and numbers as well as Satan’s false assurances of help; Satan fled when the forces met.
rows.anchor: false promises of help too that lured them away.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though Satan can be human or jinn, Islahi inclines to read the allusion here as referring to the Jews.
rows.anchor: Satan is found both among humankind and jinnkind. However, here I am inclined to believe that the reference here is to the Jews.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews feared the Prophet’s message and the scriptural prophecies that he might be the promised messenger, yet refused to accept one from outside their lineage; they indirectly stirred up the Quraysh rather than attack openly.
rows.anchor: While he was still in Makkah, they tried to instigate the Quraysh against him in various ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi considers it quite possible that the Jews urged the Quraysh to attack Madinah under cover of protecting the caravan, promising that Quraysh’s numbers and Jewish aid would defeat the Muslims.
rows.anchor: they too suggested the Quraysh to attack

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews had a treaty with the Muslims but, as 8:56–57 will show, did not honor it and continued their intrigues.
rows.anchor: they never abided by it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the armies met, the Jews were stunned by Muslim morale, and fear of the Prophet’s status and of prophecies that he would come with angels became active.
rows.anchor: Their scriptures too foretold the arrival of a prophet that he would arrive in the company of angels.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi compares Badr’s layout, number of fighters, and objective with Israel’s battle under Saul against Goliath in Samuel’s time.
rows.anchor: Badr with regard to its battle-layout, number of fighters and objective of the battle was similar to the one fought by the Israelites under Saul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects the insinuation against the Jews with the Jewish hypocrites’ false promises to fellow Jews, paralleling the account in 59:11–12.
rows.anchor: if they are attacked, they will not help them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later parable in 59:16–17 depicts Satan urging a person to disbelieve, then disowning him; both end in Hell, matching the hypocrites’ deceptive promises.
rows.anchor: these hypocrites are portrayed in a parable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an insinuates the Jews’ role instead of openly likening them to Satan because their intrigues were clandestine.
rows.anchor: pranks of the Jews were clandestine.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The allusion subtly tells the Jews that God knows their misdeeds and warns believers about their hidden enemy.
rows.anchor: they know that God is fully aware of their misdeeds. At the same time, the believers too are fore-warned of their hidden enemy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The quoted assurances and disavowal portray inner attitudes, not literal speech; Qur’anic “saying” can represent what is in the heart.
rows.anchor: The word “said” in the Qur’ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews were jealous, wanted the Quraysh to destroy the Prophet and his companions, but feared openly attacking a messenger and wanted others to bear the threat.
rows.anchor: They wanted others to bear this threat.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan entices people to sin and offers support, then abandons them when accountability approaches.
rows.anchor: he entices people to sin and offers them his support but when the time comes, he turns on his heels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who urge others to commit crimes while avoiding them themselves are culpable accomplices and share their followers’ fate, as the parable in 59:16–17 states.
rows.anchor: accomplices to crime are also culpable and will be seized for it. In fact, they reach the same fate as their followers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi applies this Satanic pattern to the Jews: they stirred the Quraysh to fight the believers but did not join the battle because they feared divine punishment.
rows.anchor: They even instigated the Quraysh to war against the believers but never participated in it themselves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When “ailment” is paired with hypocrisy, it means jealousy.
rows.anchor: When the word “ailment” is used with “hypocrisy”, it means

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where 13:41 warned Quraysh and promised Muslim success indirectly, Surah Ibrāhīm states both warning and glad tidings explicitly.
rows.anchor: the Quryash were threatened by the words “Do they not see that We are closing in upon this territory by reducing it from its borders?”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh’s evil message is rootless like a tree grown from filth and will soon be removed by those God has sent to uproot it.
rows.anchor: It is like an evil tree that has grown from garbage and dirt. It does not have any roots

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islam’s message is a deeply rooted evergreen tree; God will strengthen believers in this life and the Hereafter if they persevere in delivering truth and trust Him through trials.
rows.anchor: example of Islam’s message is that of an evergreen tree which is very deeply rooted and whose branches are spread in the sky.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ and other prophets’ stories reinforce the theme; Abraham’s migration, prayer for Arabia, and hopes for his descendants mirror Quraysh’s history and what was expected of them.
rows.anchor: migration from his homeland to the desolate desert of Arabia is referred to and the supplication he offered for this land is alluded to.

words: لِتُخْرِجَ ٱلنَّاسَ مِنَ ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ إِلَى ٱلنُّورِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is revealed to the Prophet so that, by God’s leave, he may lead people from evil beliefs and deeds into true faith and righteous action.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān has been revealed so the he can take people out from the darkness of their evil beliefs and misdeeds to the light

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After stating the Qur’an’s purpose, the passage gives the fate of those who reject it and threatens Quraysh.
rows.anchor: After that the fate of people who will reject it is stated. The Quraysh are threatened that by revealing the Qur’ ān
